title: Gotama

teacherSummary.text: In the grove of Jetavana, Siddhartha and Govinda hear Gotama teach. Govinda joins the Buddha's followers. Siddhartha deeply admires Gotama but explains to him that enlightenment cannot be taught in words; each person must find it alone. Gotama warns him gently against too much cleverness, and Siddhartha leaves, feeling Gotama has taken his friend but given him himself.

significance: The parting of friends dramatizes the novel's thesis that wisdom must be lived, not adopted.

segments.script: Today's words: novices — beginners in a religious order; discard — to reject; to throw away; enticed — tempted; attracted; venerated — regard with feelings of respect and reverence; consider hallowed or exalted or be in awe of; exhaled — expel air. “novices”: From Middle English novice, novys, from Anglo-Norman novice, Middle French novice, itself borrowed from Latin novīcius, later novitius "new, newly arrived" (in Late Latin - as a noun, masculine novicius, feminine novicia "one who has newly entered a monastery or a convent"), from novus "new". “discard”: dis- "away" + card (playing card): originally "to throw a card out of one's hand," then "to cast off." “venerated”: From Latin venerari "to revere, worship," related to venus "love, desire." (Not from venire "to come.") “exhaled”: From Middle French exhaler, from Latin exhalare, from ex "out" + halare "to breathe".

criticalVoices.quote: The result, paradoxically, is that the only way for Siddhartha to live according to the Buddha’s teaching is by choosing not to follow him, just as he eventually rejects all of the teachers he encounters, starting with his father.
criticalVoices.speaker: Jon Hughes, scholar of German literature
criticalVoices.source: "'Der Fluß des Geschehens': Time and Experience in Hermann Hesse's Demian and Siddhartha," literatur für leser 38, no. 1/15 (special issue "Forever young? Unschuld und Erfahrung im Werk Hermann Hesses," ed. Ingo Cornils), pp. 17-30, p. 23
criticalVoices.useNote: Paradox seminar: can you honor a teacher by refusing to follow him? Students compare Govinda's choice with Siddhartha's in "Gotama."
criticalVoices.linkedObjective: Analyze Siddhartha's refusal to follow Gotama: wisdom that cannot be taught.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the chapter to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
